title: "Cleanup Commands"

# Cleanup Commands

After this page you can delete merged branches, drop stashes, and remove untracked files **on purpose**.

## Merged branches

```bash
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git branch --merged
git branch -d feat/readme-note
```

`--merged` lists names whose tips are reachable from `HEAD`. `-d` refuses otherwise; `-D` deletes anyway.

Remote leftovers:

```bash
git fetch --prune
git branch -r
```

`--prune` deletes remote-tracking names that the remote no longer has.

## Stashes

```bash
git stash list
git stash drop stash@{0}
git stash clear          # every stash
```

`clear` is permanent for the stash reflog’s practical purposes. Apply first if you need the diff.

## Untracked files: `git clean`

```bash
git clean -n             # dry run
git clean -n -d          # include untracked directories
git clean -f -d          # delete
```

`-n` is mandatory the first time you run it on a tree you care about. `-f` is required (Git refuses to delete without it). `-x` also removes ignored files (build artifacts listed in `.gitignore`). That can delete `.env` if it is ignored — check `-n -x` first.

On Linux you can recover a deleted untracked file only from backups or the editor; Git never had a blob.

## Garbage collection

```bash
git gc --aggressive --prune=now
```

Packs objects, drops unreachable ones older than the prune date. Rarely needed by hand; Git runs `gc` in the background. After a huge filter-repo (chapter 20) you will run it on purpose.

## `git fsck` (peek)

```bash
git fsck --full
```

Reports dangling objects (often old amended commits) and real corruption. Dangling is normal. Missing blobs is chapter 21.
